record.tranche_reason: The study reports experiments on an alternative toy model that challenge the generality of assumptions about how superposition works, using a different loss and no element-wise nonlinearity.
record.gate_note: The results are the authors’ own toy-model experiments. The discussion of earlier work is not recorded as a result. The reported classification counts and the statement that all 100 features have some represented direction are included; no numerical results beyond those stated in the text are inferred.
record.test_reason: The post runs its own toy-model experiments on superposition: how many feature directions fit in a 2D hidden space without a ReLU under a target-only loss. It never measures neurons responding to unrelated inputs, in any model. It also does not test whether superposition causes polysemantic neurons. The construct is superposition capacity and the role of nonlinearity, which is related to V3 but different. Its results are recorded under fits_no_version rather than as a test of V3.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors say a target-only loss lets a linear toy model pack dozens of features into two dimensions. They argue nonlinearities are essential to superposition only under certain loss assumptions. They caution that toy-model results may not generalize, and say they are not confident in the findings. They also concede the loss 'is doing some heavy lifting.'
record.recipe_differences: Compared with the TMS toy model, this experiment removes the ReLU, uses 100 inputs, and trains with a loss that evaluates only the target feature rather than reconstructing the full output.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported classification accuracy depends on sparsity p: increasing sparsity improves accuracy; higher p makes clean results harder to obtain.

fits_no_version.finding: A linear toy model (100 features, 2D hidden space, target-only loss, no ReLU) represents some direction for all 100 features. At p=0.95, 31 features are accurately classified. At p=0 (no interference), more than 50 are.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Superposition of many sparse features in few dimensions does not require an element-wise nonlinearity when the loss scores only the active (target) feature; the feature count is not bounded by almost-orthogonal directions.

record.problems: The authors say the work took roughly 30 hours and that they are not confident in the findings. The experiment uses a toy model and a nonconventional loss that ignores inactive-feature reconstruction error; the text itself notes that this loss does substantial work. No quantitative uncertainty or control results are reported.
record.rows_left_out: No additional experimental outcomes are stated in the text beyond the rows listed.

untested.parts: No vision models or image-classifier neurons.
No transformer language-model MLP neurons or layer shares.

Neuron-level polysemanticity is never measured. The post does not test whether superposition causes neurons to respond to unrelated inputs. It studies only how many feature directions fit in 2D under a target-only loss.
No setting with enough neurons for every feature. No initialization, regularization or noise analysis.
No comparison of polysemantic-neuron share across activations or architectures, and no performance cost measured.
Not examined; the post's own accurate-vs-some-direction criteria concern features, not neuron labels.

record.verdict_notes: This is a quickly written LessWrong post (about 30 hours of work) with no controls or uncertainty estimates. A commenter (StefanHex) argues that ignoring inactive-feature interference makes the task unrealistically easy and not applicable to superposition; the author partly concedes. The record's V3 link is not justified, because no neuron polysemanticity is measured. The record's supports label for V3 is dropped.

versions.untested_parts: Image-classifier neurons and mixed visual inputs are not studied.
Transformer language-model neurons, tokens, contexts and layer differences are not studied.

The study tests overcomplete feature representation in a toy network, not whether natural-network neurons respond to unrelated inputs or whether superposition causes polysemanticity in trained networks generally.
The model has 100 inputs and a two-dimensional representation; the study does not test polysemanticity without capacity pressure or effects of initialization, regularization or training noise.

The study demonstrates a toy model with no element-wise nonlinearity, but does not compare polysemantic-neuron shares across activations, architectures or regularization, or measure a performance cost of reducing that share.
The study does not examine whether apparently mixed neurons detect a shared feature or whether such mixtures are rare.
The study does not compare activation-range choices or explanation-scoring methods for identifying polysemantic neurons.
